idiom_name: async function + Task/@MainActor, withCheckedContinuation and AsyncStream as bridges
implementation_notes: Swift 5.5 made the model part of the language: an async function suspends instead of blocking, Task starts 'a unit of asynchronous work' immediately and returns, and completion resumes the awaiting task in its actor context. Callback-only APIs are bridged with withCheckedContinuation (exactly-once resume) and multi-event completion with AsyncStream, so the classic completion-handler shape survives only as the wrapped API's surface. Cancellation is cooperative and threaded through the same Task.
pitfalls: Task inherits the actor context of its creation: UI state needs @MainActor/MainActor.run, otherwise the update races the main thread.
Task cancellation is cooperative - an awaited call must check Task.isCancelled or the cancellation never lands, and a cancelled task still finishes its current step.
A Task that strongly captures self keeps the object alive for the operation's lifetime; prefer [weak self] in long-running work.

variants.name: Escaping completion handler (classic Cocoa form), bridged with a continuation
variants.idiom_name: escaping (Result<T, Error>) -> Void completion + withCheckedContinuation bridge
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-5.5 shape is still everywhere in Apple's frameworks: the start call takes an @escaping completion closure that receives either the result or an error and is invoked exactly once, usually on an arbitrary queue; new async code wraps it with withCheckedContinuation so the callback becomes an awaitable continuation instead of a second code path. Keep the raw handler only for Objective-C or third-party APIs that cannot be changed, and dispatch UI work to the main actor inside it.
pitfalls: The handler must be invoked exactly once on every path: a missed path hangs the bridged continuation forever, and a double call traps with a checked continuation.
Handlers are commonly called on an arbitrary queue, so UI updates must be dispatched to the main actor explicitly.
Escaping closures that capture self create retain cycles when the operation object stores the handler.
